World.title: My Brilliant Career gets a reboot and a modern take
World.content:
Welcome to what to watch, where we take you through what's on the box in August.

This month is a mixed bag of fresh drama, an ecological thriller and the highly anticipated TV adaptation of classic Australian story My Brilliant Career. Plus, Scream King Ryan Murphy teams up with American Psycho author Bret Easton Ellis to deliver a slick new nightmare.

Here's what we're watching this month.

After Us

The Phoenix group pushed climate protest to the extreme in After Us. (Supplied: SBS)

What's it about? In a time of rising fascism and increasing technological threat, it's sometimes hard to remember that our world is also rocketing towards ecological collapse. French mini-series After Us (also known as Phoenix) will help you remember.

It's the eve of the Business Economic Ecologic forum (BEE for short), where the leaders of four of Europe's most powerful sectors — chemicals, fast fashion, banking, and oil — are gathering to announce their commitment to rewinding climate change. The jewel in their proposal is a fantastical new technology called Ice Back. It's a machine which promises to convert the carbon dioxide in the atmosphere into snow in order to reduce greenhouse gasses and re-form melted glaciers. The group intends to pledge 12 billion euros to the project which, in reality, will do less to fight climate change and more to line CEO pockets.

Fed up with the non-results from protesting, a group of young European activists kidnap the children of the four business leaders. Their demands are simple: keep the 12 billion pledge but dump the greenwashing and give the money to a real organisation fighting climate change.

From there the tight thriller unspools into a mess of attempted corporate strong-arming and radical climate action, as the sharp series asks if violence is ever justified in the face of cataclysmic environmental ruin.

Perfect for: Keeping the spark alive for the future

Where to watch: After Us premieres August 9 on SBS and SBS On Demand

Falling

Falling dances around conversations of love, lust and religion. (Supplied: ABC)

What's it about? Falling might just win the prize for most tender meet-cute of the year.

Sister Anna (Keely Hawes), cloistered in a convent outside of Bristol since the age of 16, is preparing a meal for the visiting Father David (Paapa Essiedu). During a moral argument, she burns her hand on a pot, and he holds it under cold water.

What's behind I May Destroy You? I May Destroy You and its young creator Michaela Coel are generating a helluva lot of hype. Here's what you need to know.

That simple touch — water running over their joined hands, cold English light spilling through the windows like a sign from the heavens — is enough to upend both of their lives.

Coming off the back of his smash hit Adolescence and his remake of Lord of the Flies, Jack Thorne was inspired to write his very first love story for television by a news article about a real-life nun and a priest falling in love. (Possibly this one).

But don't come into Falling thinking this is another "hot priest" show (see: Fleabag), or even a simple love story. Among the swathes of yearning, there are dark moments here. Both characters are wrestling with deep questions about their faith and their purpose, and the world outside is cruel and unrelenting.

Continually bathed in that celestial light, Essiedu is truly mesmerising any time he's on screen — he can convey a startling range of emotions through his eyes alone. Hawes infuses her deer-like vulnerability with a quiet thread of steel, and their scenes together make you hold your breath.

Occasionally weighed down by slightly overwrought speeches and the odd cliche, this series is still a compelling slow burn. Bolstering the leads are some brilliant side characters, particularly David's sister Susan (Sophie Stone). The intimate conversations between the siblings, signed in BSL, feel lived in and real.

This is a show all about love, but not just romance. The people around these two lost souls repeatedly show that belonging and community can be found both inside and outside a church.

Perfect for: Fans of I May Destroy You, Normal People, or anyone who wants some heartbreak with their hot priest

Where to watch: Falling premieres August 16 on ABC and ABC iview

My Brilliant Career

My Brilliant Career is set in the 1890s but has modern sensibilities. (Supplied: Netflix)

What's it about? There's a bittersweetness to the My Brilliant Career reboot landing on streaming weeks after the sad death of Sam Neill, the man who set so many hearts swooning in the original 1979 film.

Sam Neill's advice when the world seems dark The world has been remembering Sam Neill's incredible film and television career in the wake of the actor's death, but his off-screen antics left a robust impact.

Bitter because you're forced to reckon with the passing of time, sweet because the 2026 revamp of Miles Franklin's classic story is another gem in showrunner Liz Doran's (The Secret Life of Us, Please Like Me) own brilliant career. Sybylla (Philippa Northeast) is a young woman in 1890s Australia with perpetually ruddy cheeks, messy hair and a deep desire to rise above the societal station for women at the time. Disappointed in the opportunities her poor farming family can offer, Sybylla is sent to live with her well-to-do Granny (Anna Chancellor) in the hopes she will cast off her ideas of being a writer/artist/bohemian and settle with a suitor.

The mantle of Harry Beecham is taken up by Slow Horses star Christopher Chung, just as rugged and charming as his predecessor. Northeast sparks brightly as the fierce and ferocious Sybylla, while Doran infuses the series with modern updates and a sharp soundtrack which allow it to stand confidently against the movie.

Perfect for: People who want a Bridgerton vibe with Aussie accents

Where to watch: My Brilliant Career premieres on August 13 on Netflix

The Shards

High school is beautiful and deadly in the world of The Shards. (Supplied: Disney+)

What's it about? It's always a relief when Ryan Murphy turns his hand toward fiction as opposed to injecting his trademark lasciviousness into real-life tales of misery.

Even more so when the American Horror Story provocateur grabs onto source material that seems to be tailor-made for his dark, bombastic style: American Psycho author Bret Easton Ellis's 2023 The Shards. A fictional autobiography about Ellis's own senior year at an LA private high school, Bret (Igby Rigney) lands a soft spot for mysterious new student Robert (Homer Gere). The self-confident teen's summer romance plans are put on hold when a serial killer called The Trawler starts hacking his way through the young and beautiful of LA — and the call could be coming from inside the house!

Ellis's too-cool-for-school first person narration courtesy of Bret latches onto the neon-lit, oil slick 80's LA Murphy has created. Fans of his more bloody outings should be reassured the gore is there. The Shards also provides an excellent opportunity to rubberneck at the next generation of nepo babies with Richard Gere's son Homer taking on one of his first meatier parts, and Kaia Gerber, daughter of Cindy Crawford, clocking in for her third Murphy collab.

Perfect for: Feeling like one of the cool kids

Where to watch: The Shards premieres on August 6 on Disney+

Two Weeks in August

Two Weeks in August will have you begging for the dull comfort of your own couch. (Supplied: Robert Viglasky)

What's it about?The White Lotus: The French Riviera won't be opening its doors for at least another six months, so if you're itching for some Mike White-esque bad people-go-on-vacation time, Two Weeks in August might just be the scratch you need.

The accommodations aren't quite as luxurious as The White Lotus, but the scandals are just as hot and belaboured mum Zoe (Jessica Raine) is honestly just happy to get away from the pressures of her life. Her and her dour husband Dan (Damien Molony), head on the two-week Greek beach vacay with their friends from university and a couple of ring-ins (a much younger second wife, a lazy au pair).

An infidelity involving Dan and Jess, the second wife (Antonia Thomas) is the catalyst for barbed words, drug trips and run-ins with insufferably hilarious rich people. All the while the rage inside "people-pleaser" Zoe (or maybe she's just the only one who's not terminally selfish) bubbles along to the point of boiling over.

It's delicious to see some wonderful British bit players (You might know Molony from gone-too-soon sitcom Crashing, Thomas from Misfits or Hugh Skinner from Fleabag), stretch their legs into some truly sticky characters. But it is Raine as Zoe who steals the show, whether doing some incredible eye acting or having visions of Greek mythology (very apt for our Odyssey times) that ground the salacious story.

Perfect for: Some guilt-less judging of deplorable people

Where to watch: Two Weeks in August premieres on August 12 on Binge

World.title: Mass funeral held in Gaza for 112 people killed in Israeli strike
World.content:
The streets of Gaza City have been filled with mourners carrying the bodies of 112 Palestinians, among them more than 40 children, killed in Israeli strikes almost three years ago.

The group being laid to rest were members of two extended families in Gaza, with some gathered for the event describing it as the largest funeral in the war-ravaged strip's history.

Some of the bodies were in caskets, but most were left laying on stretchers or in body bags — each shrouded in the Palestinian flag.

Gaza's Civil Defense agency spent more than a fortnight digging through what was left of a residential block in the Sabra neighbourhood of Gaza City, which local authorities said had been destroyed in an Israeli attack in November 2023.

That was six weeks into the war, triggered by Hamas' deadly attacks on Israel on October 7 the same year.

Among the victims were 44 children and 37 women. (ABC News)

"This is the greatest remedy and healing for the people to retrieve their martyrs," local leader Nabil Al-Rifi told the ABC.

" Their families have been hoping that they will recover them so they can have a peace of mind. "

The Civil Defense believed more than 150 bodies remain trapped beneath the concrete of the building, among the thousands of Palestinians killed in the war who have never been recovered.

"We retrieved 112 bodies, the rest of the bodies we could not reach — either they had evaporated [in the blast] or they were decomposed, or the bodies were mixed up and therefore all that we could identify was 112 bodies," Mahmoud Basal, spokesperson for Gaza's Civil Defense agency told the ABC.

"Among the victims are 44 children, 37 women, 29 men, 7 elderly over 70 years old, 9 with special needs — these are shocking numbers."

Funeral 'largest in Gaza's history'

The memorial for the members of the Al Hasayna and Abu Sharia families was held on Tuesday morning, local time.

Hundreds of mourners crammed into an open area, cleared of debris, to pay their respects.

Among those farewelled were the remains of more than 40 children killed in a Gaza City neighbourhood in November 2023. (ABC News)

Banners with photos of the children who had been killed were displayed, including slogans asking for "what sin were they killed".

The remains were then marched through nearby streets, with those carrying the bodies chanting "God is great" and some firing weapons into the air.

"Today we are saying farewell to 112 martyrs, in the largest funeral in the history of the Palestinian cause," Yousef Bassam Abu Sharia, spokesperson for the Abu Sharia family told the ABC.

"Our message to the world, that cares about humanity, is that our people are facing a genocide until this moment.

"They say there is a ceasefire, but until this moment they are lying to you and our people are facing until this moment genocide and bombing day and night."

Israel has repeatedly rejected allegations of genocide in Gaza.

Israeli bombardment since Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack has reduced much of Gaza to rubble. (ABC News)

Authorities in Gaza, and some humanitarian organisations, have highlighted the difficulties in clearing destroyed areas of the strip and recovering remains due to limited heavy equipment allowed into the territory.

Israel regularly restricts such machinery, like bulldozers, citing security concerns.

"Many attempts were made to recover them, but this issue needs capabilities and equipment, and this not available in the Gaza strip because of the existing reality," the Civil Defense's Mahmoud Basal said.

"It was 17 days of work, every day eight hours of work — if we had more than one excavator, it would not have taken us such a long time."

Funeral held as debate continues over Hamas weapons

The mass funeral was set against the backdrop of significant debate over the future of Gaza, following last week's announcement by Hamas it was prepared to lay down its weapons after days of deadly attacks by Israeli forces killing around 20 Palestinians, including children.

Experts urge caution over Hamas-Israel deal Middle East analysts are sceptical Hamas will willingly lay down its weapons and that Israel will totally withdraw from Gaza.

Hamas, considered a terrorist organisation under Australian law, said it would only disarm if Israel committed to stopping attacks on Gaza and withdrawing its forces from large swathes of territory.

Hamas' agreement to hand over its weapons was made by US President Donald Trump in a social media post last Friday, where he claimed it was a proposal which had the backing of Israel.

But since then, Israeli officials have criticised the idea and suggested it was a shifting of the goalposts.

On Monday, officials from the Trump administration backed Board of Peace met with the Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Jerusalem.

Nickolay Mladenov, the Board of Peace's lead envoy for Gaza, has seemingly criticised Israel for launching strikes which killed civilians. (Reuters: Ammar Awad)

Its High Representative for Gaza, Nickolay Mladenov had seemingly criticised Israel for launching strikes which killed civilians after "intense efforts" to bring Hamas to agree to disarm.

"The meeting was constructive and detailed. Israel and the Board of Peace share a common understanding of the ultimate objectives," the Board said in a statement on X.

"The goal is clear and is not in question: the complete decommissioning of weapons in the Strip and the transition away from rule by the gun to civilian governance.

"Reaching it will be a process. And that process will be set out in the next phase of the work."

The Board of Peace insisted the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) would only withdraw to the original 'Yellow Line', the boundary of IDF controlled territory under the October 2025 ceasefire, after "decommissioning" of Hamas' weapons was complete.

"Israel has conveyed its comments and concerns on the proposed framework to our American counterparts," Doron Spielman, a spokesperson for the Israeli Prime Minister's Office told the ABC in a statement.

"The version that has been made public does not reflect Israel's positions.

"Over the past eight months, according to Israeli intelligence, Hamas has used the ceasefire to rearm, recruit thousands of additional terrorists, rebuild its military infrastructure, and prepare for further October 7-style massacres."

World.title: More than 150 migrants saved from burning boat in English Channel
World.content:
French coastguards have rescued hundreds of people from a boat that caught fire in the English Channel near the port of Boulogne-sur-Mer.

The local French administration which handles the English Channel and North Sea areas said three coastguard ships rescued 157 from the boat which was carrying migrants on Tuesday morning, local time.

There were no reported casualties.

Migration has been one of Europe's most divisive political issues since a crisis in 2015-16, when more than a million refugees and migrants — many of them fleeing war in Syria — arrived in Europe.

Last week, three people died while trying to cross the Channel on a small boat.

The latest rescue highlights the growing dangers of Channel crossings as human traffickers cram ever larger numbers of migrants onto flimsy boats.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham pledged on Sunday to be "relentless" in curbing small-boat arrivals.

The Channel is one of the world's busiest shipping lanes, and its strong currents have resulted in the deaths of many migrants trying to cross over from France to Britain.

Human traffickers typically overload their dinghies, leaving them barely afloat.

"This incident underlines the terrible dangers of small boat crossings. We continue to work relentlessly with the French and our partners overseas to prevent these perilous journeys," a British government spokesperson said.

The rescue comes shortly after Britain's right-wing Reform UK party framed its plan to stop asylum seekers from entering the country as a key election promise, which it claimed would become the largest military operation in the Channel since World War Two.

EU holds crisis talks over migrant influx

The rescue effort on the English Channel came as European interior ministers met to discuss a mass border rush in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta last week.

About 70,000 of the 72,000 migrants who entered Ceuta had left, Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said, adding that the Schengen space was never compromised as the North African enclave is not included in the agreement.

He said fellow European leaders recognised Madrid for its "immediate and efficient" response.

Mr Grande-Marlaska said Spanish intelligence had no indications a mass crossing into Ceuta was imminent.

"There was no report, no warning," he said.

" Unfortunately, these things can happen, but let's also bear in mind that we're prepared to respond immediately to a crisis of this kind. "

The minister added that Madrid had worked as fast as possible to install a maritime barrier off Ceuta's coast, following a ruling by Spain's Supreme Court in July mandating that migrants who arrived by swimming could not be immediately deported if no barrier was in place.

The influx of migrants prompted a crisis within the European Union, with Italy and Denmark among countries calling for Spain to be excluded from the bloc's free travel scheme.

Reuters

World.title: Police investigate arson on Victorian defence company as 'far left terror'
World.content:
An arson attack on a Victorian defence manufacturer last year is being investigated as an act of far-left terror.

Lovitt Industries, based in Melbourne's north-east, was targeted in July last year with three vehicles set alight and a building graffitied.

A video released after the attack, purporting to be from a group responsible for the attack, further threatened the manufacturer with a message to ""stop arming Israel or else".

Loading...

Joint counter-terror authorities have now revealed the incident is being investigated as a terror attack, "potentially orchestrated by far-left extremists with anarchist and revolutionary ideologies".

The ABC has been told it is the first time Australian authorities have investigated what they consider to be a potential far-left terror attack, motivated by anarchist and revolutionary ideology.

The counter-terror team, made up of officers from Victoria Police, the Australian Federal Police (AFP) and ASIO, have released images from the video, along with images from the attack, in the hope of identifying those responsible.

A speaker in the video, dressed in black and standing before a Palestinian flag, claims that Lovitt Technologies was targeted for supplying parts to the global F-35 fighter jet program, of which both Australia and Israel are members.

The Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team has released images of the suspects accused of targeting Lovitt Technologies last year. (Supplied: AFP)

It also included instructions on how to make similar firebombs to those used in the arson attack.

In a statement, AFP Detective Superintendent Anthony Hall said police were progressing in their investigation.

"We clearly have some information about these alleged offenders and are focused on identifying who they are,'' he said.

" We cannot overstate the seriousness of this criminality and the AFP, together with our partners, will not tolerate acts of terror motivated by extremist ideologies aiming to cause fear and anguish in our community. "

Concerns about rise in far-left terror risk

Authorities have warned of a growing concern about far-left extremism in recent years, particularly motivated by conflict in the Middle East.

The Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team has released new images of the suspects. (Supplied: AFP)

ASIO Director General Mike Burgess said in a speech to the Lowy Institute last year that while far-right extremism makes up more of ASIO's caseload, far-left extremism was a real concern.

"While nationalist and racist violent extremists make up the significant majority of our investigations into ideologically motivated extremism, events in the Middle East triggered a troubling increase in anarchist and revolutionary extremism, which is also straining cohesion," he said in November last year.

"Since October 2023, we've seen more provocative protests and a notable uptick in intentionally disruptive and damaging tactics by anti-Israel activists, including multiple acts of arson, vandalism and violent protest against defence companies accused of supplying weapon components."

Secretary of State Marco Rubio has called for countries to collaborate on efforts to counter what it described as a growing threat of far-left terror. (Reuters: Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

Last month US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, hosted a summit in Washington DC calling for countries to collaborate on efforts to counter what was described as a growing threat of far-left terror.

The summit was criticised by some as politically partisan, including by Democrats within the US, given it gave no similar regard to concerns about far-right terror.

Australia was represented at the conference by an embassy official.

A government source said there was no connection between this announcement and the Trump administration's push on far left extremism, saying the Australian government made the assessment on its own merits.

World.title: Five dead in Moscow region as Kyiv targets more Wildberries sites
World.content:
A drone strike on an industrial zone outside the Russian capital has killed five people and wounded 10 others, the region's governor said, as Moscow and Kyiv traded attacks.

Ukraine has conducted long-range strikes targeting civilian infrastructure in Russia, and in recent weeks stepped up attacks on warehouses belonging to the Russian e-commerce giant Wildberries.

Ukraine often fires hundreds of drones into Russia each night, in retaliation for Russia launching hundreds of its own drones and dozens of missiles at Ukrainian towns and cities.

Moscow's regional governor Andrey Vorobyov said early Tuesday, local time, that several fires broke out following a drone strike in the Novoselki industrial zone outside the Russian capital.

"According to preliminary information, five people were killed," he said on Telegram, adding 10 others were wounded.

Drones also damaged a warehouse near Krasny Bor in northwestern Russia, wounding one person, according to Leningrad regional governor Aleksandr Drozdenko.

Wildberries said that a fire broke out at its Krasny Bor logistics facility as a result of the attack.

Russian President Vladimir Putin is continuing to insist Russia will continue its operations in Ukraine despite a growing number of high-profile strikes. (AP: Alexander Kazakov/Sputnik)

Another Wildberries warehouse was targeted by a Ukrainian drone attack in the rural area of Emmaus, around 180 kilometres (112 miles) northwest of Moscow, regional governor Vitaly Korolyov said.

Wildberries is a highly popular online retail platform in Russia, often dubbed the "Russian Amazon", accounting for up to 10 per cent of the country's entire retail turnover, according to Russian media.

Since the start of the Ukraine war in 2022, Wildberries has been accused of helping Russians dodge Western sanctions by importing branded goods via third party countries.

Tuesday's strikes are the latest in a series of prominent drone attacks carried out by Ukraine against targets in Russia, as part of a campaign to pressure Russian President Vladimir Putin to the negotiating table.

On Monday, Russian authorities said 11 people were killed by drone strikes on a popular Russian holiday spot and on the Crimean Peninsula.

Two children killed

In Ukraine, Russian attacks killed three people in Sumy in the country's north-east, the head of the regional military administration said on Tuesday.

"Two children and an elderly woman were killed in Russian [guided aerial bomb] strikes on Sumy tonight," Oleg Grygorov said on Telegram.

"The girls were 5 and 10 years old. The children's bodies were recovered from under the rubble of their house."

Ukraine drones hit Russian holiday spot At least 11 people are dead and dozens are wounded after Ukrainian strikes on a Russian beach resort and the Crimean Peninsula.

Six guided aerial bombs struck civilian infrastructure in the city, including residential and non-residential buildings, Grygorov said.

Another attack on the port city of Mykolaiv in southern Ukraine killed an 89-year-old woman, according to Georgy Reshetilov, head of the region's military administration.

Russia launched 136 drones at Ukraine overnight, Kyiv's air force said, 117 of which were shot down or intercepted.

There has been an uptick in civilian deaths in the conflict throughout 2026, the United Nations has reported, as the four-and-a-half-year war grinds on with no sign of a peace deal.

Russia launched its full-scale offensive against Ukraine in February 2022, and has regularly struck its neighbour, including from the Crimean peninsula.

Moscow-installed authorities in Crimea on Tuesday said an unidentified soldier opened fire, killing a fellow serviceman and three civilians.

Ukraine's front lines were little changed in July as its forces largely stalled Russia's momentum, according to AFP analysis of data from the Institute for the Study of War.

AFP

World.title: Solar costs for business to be slashed under energy scheme expansion
World.content:
The cost of installing solar at schools, supermarkets, factories and farm buildings will be slashed by about 20 per cent under the expansion of a federal government scheme.

Speech excerpts seen by the ABC show Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen will announce the expansion of the Small-scale Renewable Energy Scheme (SRES) from 100 kilowatts to one megawatt during an address at the National Press Club.

The government estimates retailers could save almost $70,000 installing a 250kW solar system and a large retail complex or logistics warehouse could save more than $230,000 on a 850kW system.

The move comes after households and businesses took up batteries in droves after the introduction of the Cheaper Home Batteries Program in 2025, which allowed a subsidy worth about 30 per cent of the up-front cost of a system to be claimed.

The program has breathed new life into residential solar installations, which began to lag last year but have since picked up. Almost 4.5 million households now have rooftop solar.

Chris Bowen will unveil the expanded solar scheme during a major address. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

In the speech, Mr Bowen will note that many residential solar panels are visible from an aeroplane over a capital city, but that very few can be seen on industrial buildings.

"The missing middle is mid-scale solar," he will say.

" Factories, warehouses, farming sheds and large industrial premises — big, empty roof space ripe for solar generation. "

The 'missing middle'

Under the SRES, solar installations generate certificates that are traded on the open market.

But businesses and farmers have struggled to benefit from the scheme since its inception in 2011 because it does not apply to systems beyond 100kW, which is sufficient for a house but not a factory or large shed.

According to the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis, Australia's residential solar capacity sits at about 22 gigawatts, but businesses have only installed 5.6 gigawatts, most of which is accounted for by rooftop systems below 100kW.

The government expects businesses to not only adopt more solar amid the scheme expansion, but also have their electricity bills lowered.

"The technical rooftop potential for solar on commercial, industrial and agricultural rooftops could exceed 80 gigawatts. That's an opportunity we should miss no longer," Mr Bowen will say.

"This isn't just about energy bills, it's good for productivity, freeing up capital to invest back in their business."

Residential solar has been hugely popular in Australia. (ABC News: Daniel Mercer)

Mr Bowen will also ask the Australian Energy Market Commision to ensure network providers approve commercial and industrial solar more quickly.

See Saw Wine business development manager Maggie Jarrett welcomes that change.

The New South Wales Central Coast winery has installed 30kW of solar across three farms and is looking to add more.

"Red tape has been a massive barrier for us and just trying to understand the complexity behind that red tape, when you are an agricultural business, is difficult, especially small and medium businesses," Ms Jarrett said.

She said any reduction in up-front costs would also help.

"A 20 per cent reduction is a massive amount when you're looking at 1-megawatt solar panel developments, probably enough, as well, to enable that kind of business case to your banks to be able to get loans," Ms Jarrett said.

"I think the other piece is that it's indicating that the government supports this sort of development, which always makes financial people kind of put their ears up and say, 'Hey, if the government's backing it, there's probably more opportunity in this space.'"

Industry push amid renewable target headwinds

Several analysts have predicted that Australia will not reach its target of 82 per cent of electricity being generated by renewable energy by 2030, but in recent months Mr Bowen has said he is confident it will be achieved.

There has long been an industry push for more to be done to unlock the solar potential for businesses but approval delays and the up-front cost of systems has prevented that from eventuating.

Farmers are set to benefit from the expansion of the SRES. (ABC Landline)

Smart Energy Council policy head Rob Potter said the SRES expansion was a "game changer", particularly when coupled with the government's battery subsidy program.

"Adding solar to commercial and industrial rooftops is the equivalent to 10 coal-fired power stations," he said.

" When small and medium businesses can permanently slash their own electricity bills … then they'll increase their profits, their competitiveness and create more jobs. "

Australian Conservation Foundation climate policy advisor Annika Reynolds welcomed the announcement, but said increasing renewable energy uptake was not enough on its own.

"The Albanese government isn't nailing it when it comes to fossil fuel exports, but on the domestic renewables front it's just about bang on," she said.

"However, pressing down on the accelerator for renewables alone is unlikely to get Australia to 82 per cent renewables by 2030, which is what we need for a safe climate and an energy independent grid.

"We urge the Albanese government to explore every possible lever to firming up the closures of remaining coal and gas clunkers in Australia."

World.title: The Perth suburbs where power bills cost less than a small cup of coffee
World.content:
NationalWARenewables The Perth suburbs where power bills cost less than a small cup of coffee Indigo Lemay-Conway August 5, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Outer Perth suburbs are leading the way for postcodes with the most home battery installations over the past year. More than 50,000 batteries have been installed through the federal government’s Cheaper Home Batteries program which aims to help households store more cheap solar energy and use it when needed most. Bedfordale residents David and Ellen Gibbs with their new home battery system. Indigo Lemay Conway From April to June this year, Western Australians added enough solar capacity to power 25,000 homes – a new state record. Armadale suburbs topped the list with 2007 batteries installed across the local government area in the past 12 months.



Bedfordale residents David and Ellen Gibbs installed their system in March and have saved almost 50 per cent in power bills to date. The husband and wife duo regularly foster children, with up to 10 kids living in the house at one time. They say the home battery has been a life changer. “There’s always two adults [in the house], but the children vary because we foster. So it goes from five to 10 kids. Some of our bills were up around $1200 to $1400,” David said. “We’re using more power now because we’ve actually had to put two heat pumps in on each end of the house, so we’re using more power, [but because of the batteries] it’s costing us less, so it is a pretty significant gain.” David said their two 20 kilowatt-hour batteries would have cost them $32,000, but thanks to state and federal government rebates, 50 per cent of the bill was covered.



Their most recent power bill has set them back $650, even with higher electricity usage. In December, the federal government announced it would expand its program to an estimated $7.2 billion over the next four years. The program aims to see more than two million Australians install a battery by 2030, delivering around 40 gigawatt hours of additional storage capacity. As part of the program, home owners are eligible for a discount of around 30 per cent for a range of batteries across different sizes. In May, the state government launched its WA Residential Battery Scheme which provides access to an additional rebate and a no-interest loan to purchase and install a battery to power their homes.



Armadale resident Linda Slob’s most recent power bill cost her less than a small cup of coffee. Indigo Lemay Conway Applicants are eligible for a $1300 rebate for Synergy customers and $3800 for Horizon Power customers. Armadale residents Linda and Danny Slob have been adding solar and batteries to their home gradually over time. Their current system is now 7.2 kilowatt solar and 19.3 kWh battery, with backup power function providing energy independence in the event of a power outage. “My biggest aim was to first make the home purposeful for us because we work from home, and secondly, to ensure that we weren’t paying high bills because of our age,” Linda said.



The duo has a modular battery system and originally started out two years ago with four batteries and one inverter which set them back around $15,000. Then around six months ago, they decided to double their setup for $12,000, but this time received a rebate of around $5000. Before installing the rooftop solar and batteries, the Slob’s power bills came in around $1000 per cycle. Now they cost less than a cup of coffee. “All I know is it only cost us about $3.60 for our last bill, apart from the normal service charges,” Slob said. “I’ve actually bought a little hybrid Rav4 Toyota GR, and I’m charging that with the batteries.



Bedfordale residents David and Ellen Gibbs have halved their power bills thanks to their new solar battery. Indigo Lemay Conway “They gave me a full tank of fuel, and I haven’t even used it yet.” Other local government areas with a big uptick in home batteries installed this year include Cockburn with 1660 installs; Wanneroo at 1555 installs; Canning at 1422; and Mandurah wrapping up the top-five list with 1233 batteries installed. West State Electrics senior energy consultant Christopher Barnes said he’s seen an increase of 500 per cent for people installing more battery systems in their homes. “I’ve been doing solar for 11 years, and I think over the five years that batteries were quite exciting and new, we maybe sold 1000 kilowatt-hours of battery, and in the last 14 months, I think we must have done about 10,000 kilowatt-hours as a company already, so the uptake is insane,” he said.



Barnes said cost-of-living is one of the reasons why Perth’s outer-suburb residents have opted to install batteries more than inner-city suburbs. “I think where people are struggling the most, people are searching for financial relief, and those who are struggling the most benefit from the rebates the most,” he said. “Not everybody has $10,000 just sitting there waiting to spend on something, so having that government assistance and then also the WA interest free rebate that really makes a massive difference.” Assistant Minister for Climate Change and Energy Josh Wilson echoed similar sentiments. “The strongest uptake is happening in some of WA’s fastest-growing suburban communities,



where families are looking for practical ways to cut bills and get more value from their rooftop solar,” he said. “At a time when cost-of-living pressures remain front-of-mind, batteries are helping households keep more of the free energy they generate and reduce their reliance on expensive power from the grid.”

Welcome to the new-look Superquiz! Easier to play on your mobile, the new quiz features a fresh design and more interactive features. Click here to tell us what you think of the new format. Got questions or want to know more? Scroll past the quiz to see our FAQs. By Harry Hollinsworth



Why has the quiz changed? Our new quiz format is faster, smoother and easier to play on your mobile. We’ve also introduced several new features. For the first time, you’ll see how other players scored in real time and be able to share your result with friends and family on Facebook, X and WhatsApp. We have more exciting updates on the horizon too. Tell us what you think about the new experience here. We’re keen to hear from you. Although it has a new look, this is the same Superquiz you know and love. Our regular quizmaster is excited to put your general knowledge to the test with a new set of 15 crafty questions every day.



Can I see the number of questions in the quiz? Yes, the total number of questions is displayed next to the progress bar at the top of the quiz. The number of your current question is also shown (e.g. 3/15). Want to keep track of your score? You can find a running tally in green at the top right of the quiz. Can I see all the quiz questions at a glance? No, we challenge players to complete the quiz one question at a time.



When I answer a question, there’s a percentage next to the correct and incorrect answers. Why? Thanks for noticing! This is a new addition to the quiz. It lets you track how your score compares to other readers by showing the percentage of players who chose that particular answer. It will also help you gauge the difficulty of each question after you’ve answered. Can I reset the quiz for other players on my device? Yes, click or tap ‘Play Again’ at the end of the results screen to reset the quiz.

Two in five year 3 students in Queensland have failed to meet national NAPLAN numeracy benchmarks, months after the state began a numeracy screening trial for year 1 children. The Australian Curriculum, Assessment and Reporting Authority warned a similar “clearly concerning” dip in year 3 cohorts across the country was recorded when the National Assessment Program – Literacy and Numeracy results were released on Wednesday. In Queensland, the numeracy skills of 43.3 per cent of year 3 students were classified as either “developing” or “needs additional support” – the lowest bands. Brisbane mum Katie Wilson said while her children’s NAPLAN results were “OK”, the preparation for the tests could be overwhelming. Catherine Strohfeldt Nationally, 35.9 per cent of year 3 students fell into these categories, while Victoria recorded the strongest results of any state or territory, with more than 70 per cent achieving the national benchmark.



Brisbane mum Katie Wilson said she felt her year 3 and 5 children performed “OK” in this year’s tests and had been “pretty happy” with their scores. Wilson said the pair also found the actual tests easier than they expected after a long period of training at their state school. “There’s lots of preparation – so talk around it – in the lead-up … but I also feel that that, in a way, causes anxiety,” she said. ACARA chief executive Stephen Gniel said while families should not be stressed about the point-in-time test itself, the year 3 results pointed to a national issue. “The drop in year 3 numeracy results are clearly concerning,” Gniel said.



He said the assessment authority was already reviewing its mathematics curriculum from prep through to year 2, and education ministers were rolling out “a range of measures”, including national year 1 numeracy checks. In Queensland, year 1 students at 62 schools were screened for their numeracy ability at the start of 2026. A Queensland Education Department spokesperson said the screening was expected to find weaknesses in numeracy “as early as possible, so assistance can be provided before learning gaps widen”. When asked by this masthead what resources the department had offered to teachers, schools and students, the spokesperson said it was still analysing results from the year 1 screenings and gathering additional data.



Related Article Exclusive

Education The education gap between rich and poor students is growing. These schools may have the answer “Information gathered through the number check pilot [year 1 screening], alongside teacher feedback and research findings, will help inform future decisions about the most effective ways to support numeracy development in Queensland schools,” the spokesperson said. Gniel said the NAPLAN tests also flagged weaknesses in reading scores across years 5, 7, and 9 as compared to 2025. “It is also disheartening to see disparities persisting … from our regional and remote areas, Indigenous students and those from a disadvantaged background,” he said. Just under one-quarter of students across all year levels from very remote schools nationally cleared the curriculum benchmarks for reading and numeracy by scoring in the two highest brackets, “strong” or “exceeding”.



In major cities, 70.0 and 70.8 per cent of students, respectively, cleared the national benchmarks for reading and numeracy. In Queensland, about one-third of students sitting NAPLAN tests this year lived outside major cities, compared to 21.5 per cent of Victorian students and 24.1 per cent in NSW. World.title: A third of students fail to hit NAPLAN benchmarks
World.content:
NationalVictoriaEducation A third of students fail to hit NAPLAN benchmarks Alex Crowe August 5, 2026 — 1:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One in three Australian students are failing to meet national numeracy and literacy benchmarks, but NAPLAN data shows Victorian schools are outperforming those in other states. Nationwide NAPLAN results released on Wednesday show little or no improvement on last year, with large numbers of children still struggling with the basics of learning, despite a federal push to reshape how reading and maths are taught and tested. Sunshine Primary School has seen an improvement in its NAPLAN results for year five. Jason South The results of tests sat by more than 1.2 million children around the nation in March show nearly 30 per cent were “not achieving the learning outcomes that are expected” or “working towards expectations” in numeracy, reading, writing and spelling. More than 40 per cent of participants did not reach benchmarks in grammar. The Centre for Independent Studies education researcher Trisha Jha said if NAPLAN was a “health check” of the education system, longer-term data provided the best insight.



“On the other hand, it is important to be vigilant when there is a bit of a negative trend,” she said. Year 5, 7 and 9 students’ 2026 numeracy score improved slightly compared to 2025, while Year 3 students’ average numeracy score was lower than in all four comparable years. Changes were introduced after 2022 to how NAPLAN results are measured, and testing was moved from May to March. National reading scores and writing scores were lower across all year levels in 2026 compared to 2025. In reading, the students who received the lowest score, “Needs additional support”, was 10.2 per cent, compared to 9.3 per cent in 2025. Victorian students scored higher than the national average across all disciplines for a second consecutive year and outperformed students in all other states in writing and numeracy.



Jha said Victoria had a “geographical advantage” which often saw students perform better academically than those in other states. “Victoria has something that other states don’t have, and that is to say, they have no remote and very remote communities,” Jha said. Students from urban areas performed better than those from remote regions across the disciplines and higher results tended to align with students from the highest socio-educational backgrounds. In reading, 23.1 per cent of students from very remote schools were rated as “strong” or “exceeding”, compared to 70 per cent of students from major city schools. In numeracy, 23.1 per cent of students from very remote schools were in the top two categories, compared to 70.8 per cent of students from major city schools.



Female students outperformed male students in writing, achieving average NAPLAN scores above male students in every year group. Male students generally outperformed female students in numeracy. Sunshine Primary School principal Lyn Read with year 5 students Saqeef , Ivy and Afnan. Jason South Sunshine Primary School principal Lyn Read said her “little country school in the suburbs” had seen big improvements in grade five reading and numeracy. Read said Sunshine introduced phonics in 2019, before it was mandated in Victoria, which has helped lift its reading results. “We’ve got the proof in the pudding that we’re on the right track and doing the right things,” she said.



“The main thing for us is that I have exceptional teaching staff who are passionate about education, passionate about kids, and very collaborative.” NAPLAN participation in 2026 was slightly down on 2025 due to disruptions caused by teachers taking industrial action over wages and conditions in Tasmania and flooding in the Northern Territory. Some students were forced to sit NAPLAN writing exams twice after the online platform crashed on day one of testing. The Australian Curriculum and Reporting Authority, which oversees the tests, said the disruption only impacted students in years 5, 7 and 9. Those impacted did not receive mark adjustments, but their results came with a caveat detailing the disruption.



Federal Education Minister Jason Clare pointed to Highvale Primary School and Burwood Heights Primary School in Victoria as examples of how mandating evidence-based teaching practices had paid off. Highvale Primary saw a 25 per cent increase in students exceeding at reading in year 3 and an 11.3 per cent increase in year 5 since 2023. Burwood Heights saw a 6.8 per cent increase in the proportion of students exceeding at reading in year 3 and 10.7 per cent in year 5 since 2023. Clare mandated literacy and numeracy screening as a condition for $20 billion in school funding to the states. In response, year 1 numeracy checks will be compulsory in all Victorian public primary schools from next year. “This year’s results show that in schools using explicit teaching methods, including phonics, and small-group tutoring to give kids who are struggling extra intensive help, results are going up and up,” he said. World.title: While some WA students have fallen behind in NAPLAN, others are the best in the country
World.content:
NationalWANAPLAN While some WA students have fallen behind in NAPLAN, others are the best in the country Holly Thompson August 5, 2026 — 1:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Less than half of all year 3 students in Western Australia met proficiency standards in grammar and punctuation, the latest NAPLAN data has revealed, with just under 20 per cent needing additional support. And while results have declined across all testing areas for the state’s year 3s when compared to scores in 2023, writing and numeracy have taken the biggest hit. The latest data for 2026 testing was released by the Australian Curriculum, Assessment and Reporting Authority late on Tuesday night. To meet proficiency in each area, students must score in the top two NAPLAN bands – exceeding and strong.



Scores in the bottom two bands – developing and needs additional support – means students are not yet working at the expected level for their year group. Changes to how NAPLAN results are measured were introduced after 2022, and testing was moved from May to March. Nationally, one-in-three Australian students are failing to meet national numeracy and literacy benchmarks with WA students sitting in a similar position. ACARA chief-executive Stephen Gniel said a nationwide drop in results for year 3 students in numeracy was “clearly concerning”. In WA, nearly 40 per cent of year 3 students did not reach proficiency standards.



“Education ministers are addressing this through a range of measures including the rollout of the national year 1 numeracy check,” Gniel said. “ACARA is also playing its part by reviewing the Foundation to Year 2 Mathematics curriculum at the direction of education ministers to ensure our youngest learners get the strong grounding in mathematics and numeracy they need to succeed in their education and later in life.” Federal Education Minister Jason Clare said it was good news for year 5 and high school but “year 3 maths is a different story.” “That’s why we are fixing the maths curriculum for the first three years of school,” Clare said. WA’s year 9 students excelled in numeracy, with 71.3 per cent meeting proficiency standards – the highest nationally and on par with students in the ACT.



WA Education Minister Sabine Winton said it was encouraging to see WA students’ participation in NAPLAN remained stable, with results showing the majority of students were progressing well. “It is particularly pleasing to see that our year 9 students maintained strong and exceeding proficiency across all assessment areas, with results above the national average in reading, writing and numeracy,” she said. “These results reinforce that our year 9 students are well-prepared as they head into years 10, 11 and 12 and complete their schooling. “Critically, Western Australian students also recorded gains across all test areas, our year 7 cohort improved from their year 5 results, with their average scores in numeracy, spelling and writing showing the greatest growth.” Gniel said there was a continued improvement in national numeracy, with higher NAPLAN scores on average across years 5, 7 and 9, especially among the stronger students.



“Around 29,000 more Australian students are performing at ‘exceeding’ – the highest proficiency level – in 2026 compared to 2023,” he said. “All these improvements are testament to the exceptional work and commitment of our amazing teachers, principals and school staff around the country, as well as parents and carers and the students themselves.” Winton said it was important to remember NAPLAN was only one part of the broader picture of a student’s learning. “I encourage parents and carers to speak with their child’s school or teacher to understand their child’s overall progress,” she said.

World.title: Jetstar halves number of carry-on items customers are allowed
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAviation Jetstar halves number of carry-on items customers are allowed Chris Zappone August 5, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Jetstar will halve the number of carry-on items economy-class passengers can take onto its flights and start charging fees for guaranteed space in overhead bins, even as the budget airline increases the weight allowance for bags in the cabin. The airline allows passengers on economy fares to take on one main item, which can be stowed overhead, and one smaller item under the seat in front of them. From February, passengers will be allowed just one single carry-on bag and face boarding a flight with full overhead bins if they do not pay for priority access. Want guaranteed space in the overhead compartment? You’ll have to pay for it. The new priority carry-on fees would start at $25 one-way on selected flights and could vary, Jetstar said, providing a range from $25 for Launceston to Sydney and $52 from Cairns to Tokyo. Customers paying the new overhead compartment fee will get priority access by being allowed to board the plane first. Passengers who don’t pay up will still have access to the overhead bins, but only after those who pay have stowed away their carry-on bags.



While the airline slashes the number of carry-on items passengers can take from two to one, the single carry-on bag can weigh up to 10 kilograms, up from the current limit of seven kilograms. Jetstar will require passengers to store the free item under the seat in front of them. The change means handbags, laptops, coats, blankets and umbrellas will have to fit into one bag, rather than being the second item passengers are allowed to take on board. Matt Golding The model of charging for carry-on storage is a model adapted from European no-frills carriers such as easyJet, Ryanair and Wizz Air. It’s a cash spinner, with ancillary fees such as baggage and seat selection fees generating close to a third of Ryanair’s €15.54 billion ($25.5 billion) revenue in the past financial year.



Jetstar said the luggage rule change was aimed at speeding up boarding times, which is a core concern as delays in boarding translate into delayed departures, which can cascade into other issues. “From February, the main thing customers will need to think about is the size of their carry-on,” said Jetstar chief executive Stephanie Tully. “By giving customers an underseat bag with the option to add priority carry-on, we can make better use of overhead locker space, streamline boarding and help more flights depart on time.” For passengers on existing bookings including two carry-on items for flights departing before February 2, 2027, the carry-on allowance remains unchanged. For flights departing after February 2, 2027, customers on those fares will get the priority carry-on option. Jetstar ranked as the nation’s lowest airline for on-time departures in June 2026, according to the Bureau of Infrastructure and Transport Research Economics. It posted a score of 75 per cent, compared with 80.8 per cent for Virgin and 87.8 per cent for Qantas.

World.title: Australia leads the world in rooftop solar, but only on certain roofs. Until now
World.content:
EnvironmentClimate changeRenewables Australia leads the world in rooftop solar, but only on certain roofs. Until now Nick O'Malley August 4, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Albanese government plans to push solar power to the rooftops of large businesses, factories and warehouses across Australia’s largest cities, as Labor struggles to fill what Energy Minister Chris Bowen calls the “missing middle” of its renewable energy target in the power grid. Australia has more household rooftop solar than any other nation, and large-scale solar farms, but commercial roof space in cities has been largely left out of the race due to the cost of establishing medium-sized systems and the difficulty of having them connected to the grid. A solar installation at the Moorebank Logistics terminal in western Sydney. Bowen will announce in a speech at the National Press Club on Wednesday that the rebate scheme that helped households install solar will be expanded to include systems of up to 1 megawatt. It is currently capped at 100-kilowatt systems. Bowen will also ask the Australian Energy Market Commission to consider a rule change requiring the network providers – companies that own the poles and wires – to approve and connect commercial and industrial solar faster.



“Many of you in this room have to spend plenty of time on aeroplanes for work,” Bowen will say, according to a draft of his speech. Related Article Opinion

Climate policy Rewarding companies to do nothing is undermining Australia’s climate cuts Caitlin Fitzsimmons Environment and climate reporter “You might have noticed when you come in to land the prevalence of solar on residential rooftops – you’d see more solar panels than backyard pools. But have you also noticed that many warehouse and factory roofs are devoid of solar panels, or only have panels covering a fairly small percentage of the roof space? “The missing middle is mid-scale solar. Factories, warehouses, farming sheds and large industrial premises – big empty roof space ripe for solar generation.” While 22 gigawatts of energy is generated from solar on Australian residential properties, businesses have installed only about 5.6 gigawatts.



Bowen will say the potential for solar on commercial rooftops could exceed 80 gigawatts. He estimates the added incentives, to start in October, will cut the cost of installing a medium-sized solar system by about 20 per cent. “Take, for example, the installation of a 250kW solar system on a medium-sized enterprise, like a retailer. Upfront they could save about $68,000 on installation,” Bowen will say. “But going forward they’d be generating about 345 megawatt hours of electricity each year, a potential saving of $50,000 in annual electricity costs. Bowen will also make it a priority to get solar installations for businesses moving more quickly. “While I understand these can be complex questions that need to be worked through, many of the delays I have heard about are unacceptable and simply make it so hard for businesses to install solar that they just give up,” he will say.



On Monday, renewables sector peak body the Smart Energy Council released a report saying costs and the difficulty of connecting systems on commercial buildings to the grid were the leading barriers to businesses deciding to invest. The council’s head of policy, Robert Potter, said there was enough idle rooftop space to generate as much power as 10 coal-fired power plants. Australia has more household rooftop solar panels than any other nation. Eamon Gallagher “For a small or medium business, the difference between an upfront, certain incentive and a progressively priced one can be the difference between a project stacking up and one that doesn’t,” Potter said. The acting chief executive of Energy Networks Australia, Dominic Adams, said the group welcomed the widening of the incentive.



“Networks are continually improving connection processes to make them clearer, faster and more consistent for customers,” he said. Related Article Recycling Millions of solar panels go to landfill. Why aren’t they recycled? The Albanese government is struggling in its race towards 82 per cent renewables in the grid by 2030, amid growing resistance from the Coalition and some community groups to large renewable projects and associated transmission lines. But even leading opponents of renewables, like One Nation’s Barnaby Joyce, have voiced support for rooftop solar. The Australian Conservation Foundation welcomed the policy as part of the government’s efforts to reduce emissions.



“The Albanese government isn’t nailing it when it comes to fossil fuel exports, but on the domestic renewables front – it’s just about bang on,” the foundation’s national climate policy adviser, Annika Reynolds, said. “ACF has long championed the expansion of federal schemes to better unlock rooftop solar for commercial premises. Rooftop solar is a win-win – it’s good for nature, and good for people.” Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: The Perth suburbs where power bills cost less than a small cup of coffee
World.content:
NationalWARenewables The Perth suburbs where power bills cost less than a small cup of coffee Indigo Lemay-Conway August 5, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Outer Perth suburbs are leading the way for postcodes with the most home battery installations over the past year. More than 50,000 batteries have been installed through the federal government’s Cheaper Home Batteries program which aims to help households store more cheap solar energy and use it when needed most. Bedfordale residents David and Ellen Gibbs with their new home battery system. Indigo Lemay Conway From April to June this year, Western Australians added enough solar capacity to power 25,000 homes – a new state record. Armadale suburbs topped the list with 2007 batteries installed across the local government area in the past 12 months.



Bedfordale residents David and Ellen Gibbs installed their system in March and have saved almost 50 per cent in power bills to date. The husband and wife duo regularly foster children, with up to 10 kids living in the house at one time. They say the home battery has been a life changer. “There’s always two adults [in the house], but the children vary because we foster. So it goes from five to 10 kids. Some of our bills were up around $1200 to $1400,” David said. “We’re using more power now because we’ve actually had to put two heat pumps in on each end of the house, so we’re using more power, [but because of the batteries] it’s costing us less, so it is a pretty significant gain.” David said their two 20 kilowatt-hour batteries would have cost them $32,000, but thanks to state and federal government rebates, 50 per cent of the bill was covered.



Their most recent power bill has set them back $650, even with higher electricity usage. In December, the federal government announced it would expand its program to an estimated $7.2 billion over the next four years. The program aims to see more than two million Australians install a battery by 2030, delivering around 40 gigawatt hours of additional storage capacity. As part of the program, home owners are eligible for a discount of around 30 per cent for a range of batteries across different sizes. In May, the state government launched its WA Residential Battery Scheme which provides access to an additional rebate and a no-interest loan to purchase and install a battery to power their homes.



Armadale resident Linda Slob’s most recent power bill cost her less than a small cup of coffee. Indigo Lemay Conway Applicants are eligible for a $1300 rebate for Synergy customers and $3800 for Horizon Power customers. Armadale residents Linda and Danny Slob have been adding solar and batteries to their home gradually over time. Their current system is now 7.2 kilowatt solar and 19.3 kWh battery, with backup power function providing energy independence in the event of a power outage. “My biggest aim was to first make the home purposeful for us because we work from home, and secondly, to ensure that we weren’t paying high bills because of our age,” Linda said.



The duo has a modular battery system and originally started out two years ago with four batteries and one inverter which set them back around $15,000. Then around six months ago, they decided to double their setup for $12,000, but this time received a rebate of around $5000. Before installing the rooftop solar and batteries, the Slob’s power bills came in around $1000 per cycle. Now they cost less than a cup of coffee. “All I know is it only cost us about $3.60 for our last bill, apart from the normal service charges,” Slob said. “I’ve actually bought a little hybrid Rav4 Toyota GR, and I’m charging that with the batteries.



Bedfordale residents David and Ellen Gibbs have halved their power bills thanks to their new solar battery. Indigo Lemay Conway “They gave me a full tank of fuel, and I haven’t even used it yet.” Other local government areas with a big uptick in home batteries installed this year include Cockburn with 1660 installs; Wanneroo at 1555 installs; Canning at 1422; and Mandurah wrapping up the top-five list with 1233 batteries installed. West State Electrics senior energy consultant Christopher Barnes said he’s seen an increase of 500 per cent for people installing more battery systems in their homes. “I’ve been doing solar for 11 years, and I think over the five years that batteries were quite exciting and new, we maybe sold 1000 kilowatt-hours of battery, and in the last 14 months, I think we must have done about 10,000 kilowatt-hours as a company already, so the uptake is insane,” he said.



Barnes said cost-of-living is one of the reasons why Perth’s outer-suburb residents have opted to install batteries more than inner-city suburbs. “I think where people are struggling the most, people are searching for financial relief, and those who are struggling the most benefit from the rebates the most,” he said. “Not everybody has $10,000 just sitting there waiting to spend on something, so having that government assistance and then also the WA interest free rebate that really makes a massive difference.” Assistant Minister for Climate Change and Energy Josh Wilson echoed similar sentiments. “The strongest uptake is happening in some of WA’s fastest-growing suburban communities,



where families are looking for practical ways to cut bills and get more value from their rooftop solar,” he said. “At a time when cost-of-living pressures remain front-of-mind, batteries are helping households keep more of the free energy they generate and reduce their reliance on expensive power from the grid.”

World.content:
NationalSuperquiz Superquiz, Wednesday, August 5 August 5, 2026 — 1:07am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Welcome to the new-look Superquiz! Easier to play on your mobile, the new quiz features a fresh design and more interactive features. Click here to tell us what you think of the new format. Got questions or want to know more? Scroll past the quiz to see our FAQs. By Harry Hollinsworth



Why has the quiz changed? Our new quiz format is faster, smoother and easier to play on your mobile. We’ve also introduced several new features. For the first time, you’ll see how other players scored in real time and be able to share your result with friends and family on Facebook, X and WhatsApp. We have more exciting updates on the horizon too. Tell us what you think about the new experience here. We’re keen to hear from you. Although it has a new look, this is the same Superquiz you know and love. Our regular quizmaster is excited to put your general knowledge to the test with a new set of 15 crafty questions every day.



Can I see the number of questions in the quiz? Yes, the total number of questions is displayed next to the progress bar at the top of the quiz. The number of your current question is also shown (e.g. 3/15). Want to keep track of your score? You can find a running tally in green at the top right of the quiz. Can I see all the quiz questions at a glance? No, we challenge players to complete the quiz one question at a time.



When I answer a question, there’s a percentage next to the correct and incorrect answers. Why? Thanks for noticing! This is a new addition to the quiz. It lets you track how your score compares to other readers by showing the percentage of players who chose that particular answer. It will also help you gauge the difficulty of each question after you’ve answered. Can I reset the quiz for other players on my device? Yes, click or tap ‘Play Again’ at the end of the results screen to reset the quiz.
