Students from urban areas performed better than those from remote regions across the disciplines and higher results tended to align with students from the highest socio-educational backgrounds. In reading, 23.1 per cent of students from very remote schools were rated as “strong” or “exceeding”, compared to 70 per cent of students from major city schools. In numeracy, 23.1 per cent of students from very remote schools were in the top two categories, compared to 70.8 per cent of students from major city schools.



Female students outperformed male students in writing, achieving average NAPLAN scores above male students in every year group. Male students generally outperformed female students in numeracy. Sunshine Primary School principal Lyn Read with year 5 students Saqeef , Ivy and Afnan. Jason South Sunshine Primary School principal Lyn Read said her “little country school in the suburbs” had seen big improvements in grade five reading and numeracy. Read said Sunshine introduced phonics in 2019, before it was mandated in Victoria, which has helped lift its reading results. “We’ve got the proof in the pudding that we’re on the right track and doing the right things,” she said.



“The main thing for us is that I have exceptional teaching staff who are passionate about education, passionate about kids, and very collaborative.” NAPLAN participation in 2026 was slightly down on 2025 due to disruptions caused by teachers taking industrial action over wages and conditions in Tasmania and flooding in the Northern Territory. Some students were forced to sit NAPLAN writing exams twice after the online platform crashed on day one of testing. The Australian Curriculum and Reporting Authority, which oversees the tests, said the disruption only impacted students in years 5, 7 and 9. Those impacted did not receive mark adjustments, but their results came with a caveat detailing the disruption.



Federal Education Minister Jason Clare pointed to Highvale Primary School and Burwood Heights Primary School in Victoria as examples of how mandating evidence-based teaching practices had paid off. Highvale Primary saw a 25 per cent increase in students exceeding at reading in year 3 and an 11.3 per cent increase in year 5 since 2023. Burwood Heights saw a 6.8 per cent increase in the proportion of students exceeding at reading in year 3 and 10.7 per cent in year 5 since 2023. Clare mandated literacy and numeracy screening as a condition for $20 billion in school funding to the states. In response, year 1 numeracy checks will be compulsory in all Victorian public primary schools from next year. “This year’s results show that in schools using explicit teaching methods, including phonics, and small-group tutoring to give kids who are struggling extra intensive help, results are going up and up,” he said. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: While some WA students have fallen behind in NAPLAN, others are the best in the country
World.content:
NationalWANAPLAN While some WA students have fallen behind in NAPLAN, others are the best in the country Holly Thompson August 5, 2026 — 1:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Less than half of all year 3 students in Western Australia met proficiency standards in grammar and punctuation, the latest NAPLAN data has revealed, with just under 20 per cent needing additional support. And while results have declined across all testing areas for the state’s year 3s when compared to scores in 2023, writing and numeracy have taken the biggest hit. The latest data for 2026 testing was released by the Australian Curriculum, Assessment and Reporting Authority late on Tuesday night. To meet proficiency in each area, students must score in the top two NAPLAN bands – exceeding and strong.



Scores in the bottom two bands – developing and needs additional support – means students are not yet working at the expected level for their year group. Changes to how NAPLAN results are measured were introduced after 2022, and testing was moved from May to March. Nationally, one-in-three Australian students are failing to meet national numeracy and literacy benchmarks with WA students sitting in a similar position. ACARA chief-executive Stephen Gniel said a nationwide drop in results for year 3 students in numeracy was “clearly concerning”. In WA, nearly 40 per cent of year 3 students did not reach proficiency standards.



“Education ministers are addressing this through a range of measures including the rollout of the national year 1 numeracy check,” Gniel said. “ACARA is also playing its part by reviewing the Foundation to Year 2 Mathematics curriculum at the direction of education ministers to ensure our youngest learners get the strong grounding in mathematics and numeracy they need to succeed in their education and later in life.” Federal Education Minister Jason Clare said it was good news for year 5 and high school but “year 3 maths is a different story.” “That’s why we are fixing the maths curriculum for the first three years of school,” Clare said. WA’s year 9 students excelled in numeracy, with 71.3 per cent meeting proficiency standards – the highest nationally and on par with students in the ACT.



WA Education Minister Sabine Winton said it was encouraging to see WA students’ participation in NAPLAN remained stable, with results showing the majority of students were progressing well. “It is particularly pleasing to see that our year 9 students maintained strong and exceeding proficiency across all assessment areas, with results above the national average in reading, writing and numeracy,” she said. “These results reinforce that our year 9 students are well-prepared as they head into years 10, 11 and 12 and complete their schooling. “Critically, Western Australian students also recorded gains across all test areas, our year 7 cohort improved from their year 5 results, with their average scores in numeracy, spelling and writing showing the greatest growth.” Gniel said there was a continued improvement in national numeracy, with higher NAPLAN scores on average across years 5, 7 and 9, especially among the stronger students.



“Around 29,000 more Australian students are performing at ‘exceeding’ – the highest proficiency level – in 2026 compared to 2023,” he said. “All these improvements are testament to the exceptional work and commitment of our amazing teachers, principals and school staff around the country, as well as parents and carers and the students themselves.” Winton said it was important to remember NAPLAN was only one part of the broader picture of a student’s learning. “I encourage parents and carers to speak with their child’s school or teacher to understand their child’s overall progress,” she said.

World.title: Jetstar halves number of carry-on items customers are allowed
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAviation Jetstar halves number of carry-on items customers are allowed Chris Zappone August 5, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Jetstar will halve the number of carry-on items economy-class passengers can take onto its flights and start charging fees for guaranteed space in overhead bins, even as the budget airline increases the weight allowance for bags in the cabin. The airline allows passengers on economy fares to take on one main item, which can be stowed overhead, and one smaller item under the seat in front of them. From February, passengers will be allowed just one single carry-on bag and face boarding a flight with full overhead bins if they do not pay for priority access. Want guaranteed space in the overhead compartment? You’ll have to pay for it. The new priority carry-on fees would start at $25 one-way on selected flights and could vary, Jetstar said, providing a range from $25 for Launceston to Sydney and $52 from Cairns to Tokyo. Customers paying the new overhead compartment fee will get priority access by being allowed to board the plane first. Passengers who don’t pay up will still have access to the overhead bins, but only after those who pay have stowed away their carry-on bags.



While the airline slashes the number of carry-on items passengers can take from two to one, the single carry-on bag can weigh up to 10 kilograms, up from the current limit of seven kilograms. Jetstar will require passengers to store the free item under the seat in front of them. The change means handbags, laptops, coats, blankets and umbrellas will have to fit into one bag, rather than being the second item passengers are allowed to take on board. Matt Golding The model of charging for carry-on storage is a model adapted from European no-frills carriers such as easyJet, Ryanair and Wizz Air. It’s a cash spinner, with ancillary fees such as baggage and seat selection fees generating close to a third of Ryanair’s €15.54 billion ($25.5 billion) revenue in the past financial year.



Jetstar said the luggage rule change was aimed at speeding up boarding times, which is a core concern as delays in boarding translate into delayed departures, which can cascade into other issues. “From February, the main thing customers will need to think about is the size of their carry-on,” said Jetstar chief executive Stephanie Tully. “By giving customers an underseat bag with the option to add priority carry-on, we can make better use of overhead locker space, streamline boarding and help more flights depart on time.” For passengers on existing bookings including two carry-on items for flights departing before February 2, 2027, the carry-on allowance remains unchanged. For flights departing after February 2, 2027, customers on those fares will get the priority carry-on option. Jetstar ranked as the nation’s lowest airline for on-time departures in June 2026, according to the Bureau of Infrastructure and Transport Research Economics. It posted a score of 75 per cent, compared with 80.8 per cent for Virgin and 87.8 per cent for Qantas.

World.title: Australia leads the world in rooftop solar, but only on certain roofs. Until now
World.content:
EnvironmentClimate changeRenewables Australia leads the world in rooftop solar, but only on certain roofs. Until now Nick O'Malley August 4, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Albanese government plans to push solar power to the rooftops of large businesses, factories and warehouses across Australia’s largest cities, as Labor struggles to fill what Energy Minister Chris Bowen calls the “missing middle” of its renewable energy target in the power grid. Australia has more household rooftop solar than any other nation, and large-scale solar farms, but commercial roof space in cities has been largely left out of the race due to the cost of establishing medium-sized systems and the difficulty of having them connected to the grid. A solar installation at the Moorebank Logistics terminal in western Sydney. Bowen will announce in a speech at the National Press Club on Wednesday that the rebate scheme that helped households install solar will be expanded to include systems of up to 1 megawatt. It is currently capped at 100-kilowatt systems. Bowen will also ask the Australian Energy Market Commission to consider a rule change requiring the network providers – companies that own the poles and wires – to approve and connect commercial and industrial solar faster.



“Many of you in this room have to spend plenty of time on aeroplanes for work,” Bowen will say, according to a draft of his speech. Related Article Opinion

Climate policy Rewarding companies to do nothing is undermining Australia’s climate cuts Caitlin Fitzsimmons Environment and climate reporter “You might have noticed when you come in to land the prevalence of solar on residential rooftops – you’d see more solar panels than backyard pools. But have you also noticed that many warehouse and factory roofs are devoid of solar panels, or only have panels covering a fairly small percentage of the roof space? “The missing middle is mid-scale solar. Factories, warehouses, farming sheds and large industrial premises – big empty roof space ripe for solar generation.” While 22 gigawatts of energy is generated from solar on Australian residential properties, businesses have installed only about 5.6 gigawatts.



Bowen will say the potential for solar on commercial rooftops could exceed 80 gigawatts. He estimates the added incentives, to start in October, will cut the cost of installing a medium-sized solar system by about 20 per cent. “Take, for example, the installation of a 250kW solar system on a medium-sized enterprise, like a retailer. Upfront they could save about $68,000 on installation,” Bowen will say. “But going forward they’d be generating about 345 megawatt hours of electricity each year, a potential saving of $50,000 in annual electricity costs. Bowen will also make it a priority to get solar installations for businesses moving more quickly. “While I understand these can be complex questions that need to be worked through, many of the delays I have heard about are unacceptable and simply make it so hard for businesses to install solar that they just give up,” he will say.



On Monday, renewables sector peak body the Smart Energy Council released a report saying costs and the difficulty of connecting systems on commercial buildings to the grid were the leading barriers to businesses deciding to invest. The council’s head of policy, Robert Potter, said there was enough idle rooftop space to generate as much power as 10 coal-fired power plants. Australia has more household rooftop solar panels than any other nation. Eamon Gallagher “For a small or medium business, the difference between an upfront, certain incentive and a progressively priced one can be the difference between a project stacking up and one that doesn’t,” Potter said. The acting chief executive of Energy Networks Australia, Dominic Adams, said the group welcomed the widening of the incentive.



“Networks are continually improving connection processes to make them clearer, faster and more consistent for customers,” he said. Related Article Recycling Millions of solar panels go to landfill. Why aren’t they recycled? The Albanese government is struggling in its race towards 82 per cent renewables in the grid by 2030, amid growing resistance from the Coalition and some community groups to large renewable projects and associated transmission lines. But even leading opponents of renewables, like One Nation’s Barnaby Joyce, have voiced support for rooftop solar. The Australian Conservation Foundation welcomed the policy as part of the government’s efforts to reduce emissions.



“The Albanese government isn’t nailing it when it comes to fossil fuel exports, but on the domestic renewables front – it’s just about bang on,” the foundation’s national climate policy adviser, Annika Reynolds, said. “ACF has long championed the expansion of federal schemes to better unlock rooftop solar for commercial premises. Rooftop solar is a win-win – it’s good for nature, and good for people.” Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: Taranaki councils vote on amalgamation - but leave New Plymouth out in the cold
World.content:
Stratford District Council has voted unanimously to pursue amalgamation with the South Taranaki District Council as part of local government reforms, at the expense of a wider union with the New Plymouth District Council.

It's the second rebuff this week for New Plymouth, after South Taranaki also voted for a two-council model - one unitary council for south-central Taranaki and one in the north.

Territorial authorities around the country have until Sunday to submit proposals ahead of the deadline for the Head Start pathway as part of reforms which will consign regional councils to history.

Stratford and South Taranaki have lost little time in making their wishes known.

Stratford mayor Neil Volzke called it a no brainer.

"When you look at the similarity of our two councils we've both got large rural areas, a number of small towns servicing those areas and our structure, our values and things that are important to us as communities are very similar."

In his opinion, New Plymouth was a whole different kettle of fish.

"When you look at New Plymouth it's more urban based, of course, and their priorities are different.

"So, it's not a one size fits all and it's not a convenience kind of discussion, it's about where you feel most naturally suited and for us that sort of rural feel versus urban is kind of a better fit."

South Taranaki mayor Phil Nixon was on the same page.

"The fact that we're rural, we're much smaller towns, that's really the difference.

South Taranaki mayor Phil Nixon. RNZ / Robin Martin

"And we don't always entirely understand what it's like to be in that urban, that city community, as I don't think a lot of them in the heart of the city always understand our problems and what we go through in the rural areas."

He said the province would still need to take a team Taranaki approach.

"We certainly need to have a good relationship. We always have. We've been Taranaki as one, and so we need to have a really good working relationship with them.

"People say in South Taranaki it's all about Hāwera. But, the way I look at it is if Hāwera is not doing well, South Taranaki doesn't do well.

"And it's the same with New Plymouth. If New Plymouth's not doing well, Taranaki doesn't do well."

For their part, the New Plymouth District Council and Taranaki Regional Council (TRC) had called in consultants to help put together a $1.3 million so-called 'Pathfinder Proposal'.

That was despite the TRC not officially being invited to make a submission.

New Plymouth mayor Max Brough admitted the strategy was not without its risks.

"Personally, I don't see anything wrong with the two-unitary councils model, but it's too early to make that call for us.

"Look, we're doing quite a bit of work. We're spending a lot of money, and I question whether that's the right thing to do now, given that South have gone out and very clearly said, no matter what the depth of the analysis is at the end, they think they want to have two unitary councils from the start."

He said the Pathfinder Proposal aimed to canvass all the options.

New Plymouth mayor Max Brough. ROBIN MARTIN / RNZ

On Stratford's Broadway there were mixed views on leaving New Plymouth out in the cold.

Dot was looking to the south.

"I think it's a good idea [to go with South Taranaki]. I don't see why we should be lumbered with New Plymouth."

Simon was for a unified approach.

"I think it should all come under one council."

A man, who preferred not to give his name, felt otherwise.

"I'd rather go south. New Plymouth will rip us off."

Margaret thought Stratford and Hāwera were a good fit.

"We're both similar, rural communities, and New Plymouth is a city."

Stratford's main street, Broadway. Wiki commons

Connor agreed.

"Stratford really aligns with South Taranaki more than it does New Plymouth."

A woman, who asked not give her name, liked the status quo.

"I think we should just leave it like it is. Nothing good comes from making things different, change."

Jessie wasn't a fan of the city to the north.

"Nah, nah, not New Plymouth. Stratford would just get lost in all the politics of the big city,"

Alan was thinking of the potential savings.

"We're better off all in one as far as reducing our costs, you know, instead of having multiple administrations having one across the whole province, just to reduce the cost for the ratepayer."

The New Plymouth District Council will vote on whether to submit its Pathfinder Proposal on Thursday.

World.title: Some rough sleepers refusing emergency accommodation despite freezing temperatures
World.content:
The Christchurch City Mission says some people sleeping rough are refusing emergency accommodation, despite freezing temperatures.

Snow and sleet hit the lower North and the South Island on Tuesday.

In Christchurch, the city mission worried that those sleeping outside could still be wet when temperatures drop below zero.

City Missioner Corinne Haines said it could not force people to accept help.

She said many experiencing homelessness had a bad experience, had been through trauma, struggled with their mental health, feared for their safety, or did not trust support services.

"When you're cold, when you're wet, when you're hungry, when you're not quite in step with society, it's very hard to make good and brave decisions, and for some of these people, leaving the street is actually a very brave decision," Haines said.

Christchurch City Missioner Corinne Haines. Supplied / Christchurch City Mission

In a Facebook post, the city mission said staff were genuinely worried they would find someone who had not survived through the night.

"That is especially so because we are seeing more elderly people now out on the streets. They came across an 82-year-old last week who, for his own reasons, chose to stay out."

Haines said it was working to build trust.

"We meet them where they are. We check in with them after a cold night or severe weather. We bring practical support for them.

"That's not ideal from our perspective. We would much sooner they came inside, and they took up our offer of support, of housing, even if it's only short-term.

World.title: Should customers pay less when they use a self-checkout?
World.content:
Who is really saving money when supermarket shoppers check out and bag their own groceries?

That is a question New York lawmakers have reportedly been pondering.

State representative Nikki Lucas has introduced a bill that would require retail businesses selling food in the state to offer a 10 percent discount to those who used the self-checkout lane.

"Retail businesses increasingly rely on self-checkout systems to reduce staffing and operational costs by shifting responsibilities traditionally performed by employees onto consumers," she wrote.

Do I have to buy that extended warranty? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 12m

"Since customers are effectively completing portions of the checkout labor themselves without compensation, providing a mandatory discount helps ensure fairness, acknowledges consumer participation in store operations, and allows the public to share in the financial savings created by self-service technology."

Consumer NZ head of advocacy Gemma Rasmussen said her organisation thought there was validity to the argument in New Zealand, too.

"If you're serving yourself then ultimately the supermarket is saving money through less staff resourcing, and those savings are not currently being passed on to shoppers.

"Pak'n Save advertises themselves as a cheaper place to shop given you pack your bags yourself. It seems many businesses are moving towards fewer staff and more technological assistance, for example there are now fewer bank branches across New Zealand, and more chatbots instead of call centre representatives across a number of major businesses. Ultimately this provides a cost saving for the business, not the consumer."

She said concern about the price of food and groceries was still the number one financial worry for most people.

"When we started tracking financial concerns in 2022, food pricing was the 8th highest concern. Lowering prices for shoppers who choose to self-serve would be one way to alleviate some of these cost pressures, however we're dubious the supermarkets would introduce such a discount."

University of Auckland marketing expert Professor Michael Lee said it made sense from a fairness point-of-view.

"The supermarkets are saving ongoing cost of labour by automating that portion of their operations. Therefore, why not to pass on the savings to their loyal customers?"

He said in a market like New Zealand, it was unlikely that retailers would make the choice to offer a discount, unless they were compelled to.

"Unless one of the retailers, or a new entrant, decided to take this approach, there would little incentive for either to do so, meaning that the two main retailers would continue to use such cost savings to extend their profit margin."

Foodstuffs said self-checkouts were one of a number of ways customers could choose to shop, alongside traditional staffed checkouts.

"Many customers value the convenience, speed and flexibility that self-service offers, particularly when buying a small number of items. We continue to invest in both self-service and staffed checkouts so customers can choose the option that best suits their needs. Team members are always available to assist customers using self-checkouts and to operate staffed lanes. Our focus is on giving customers choice and making shopping as easy and convenient as possible."

Woolworths was also approached for comment.

World.title: Work and Income security guard numbers to be cut back
World.content:
The Ministry of Social Development (MSD) is planning to cut the number of security guards at Work and Income offices throughout the country.

A security guard and unions say the changes are dangerous, threatening the safety of both security guards and staff following the murders of two Ashburton Work and Income employees in 2014.

MSD says its service centres are now safe - after it spent $80 million boosting security measures.

Twenty-two security guard jobs are set to go at 22 regional offices - reducing the number of guards at these sites from three to two.

The offices affected are Dargaville, Flaxmere, Huntly, Johnsonville, Kamo, Kāpiti, Kawakawa, Kawerau, Kerikeri, Morrinsville, Motueka, Mount Maunganui, Ōpōtiki, Paeroa, Richmond, Ruatoria, Te Awamutu, Te Puke, Tokoroa, Tūrangi, Waihi, and Wairoa, the Public Service Association said.

MSD reduced 20 security guard jobs at other Work and Income offices in March this year.

It comes as official data reveals staff have faced thousands of security incidents over the past five years, and experienced over 1700 lockdowns.

A security guard and E tū union member at an affected site, who RNZ has agreed not to name, said the cuts were "absolutely ludicrous".

A scene investigation at the Work and Income office in Ashburton after the shootings. RNZ / Jemma Brackebush

He said the Ashburton killings were always at the back of his mind, and he was worried about the safety of guards and staff members due to threats he'd dealt with.

"You can get anything from verbal abuse, to people being threatened to be killed, or people will go off disgruntled and mutter under their breath that they're going to come back with a shotgun - we've had that happen.

"We had one guy who tried to come into the office with a knife.

"It was only because the dilligence of one of our officers who saw him - and he immediately put the site into lockdown and phoned the police."

The guard said three security guards were necessary because when lockdowns arose, one guard ushered clients out the back for safety, and the other two concentrated on people causing the problem.

The killings in Ashburton prompted MSD to launch an internal review, and employ an extra 100 security guards at Work and Income centres.

WorkSafe brought charges against MSD and in 2016, Judge Jan-Marie Doogue found the ministry had failed to ensure there was no physically unrestricted access to the staff working area.

Chief District Court judge Jan-Marie Doogue listening to arguments in the case against the Ministry of Social Development at the Wellington District Court. Pool / Fairfax NZ

The Public Service Association national secretary Fleur Fitzsimmons said MSD staff had people spitting at them, throwing objects, jumping over desks, and making bomb and gun threats.

"We think [incidents] are significantly underreported - the reality is MSD workers deal with unacceptable violence and aggression from members of the public, and security guards are an important response to this, and safety initiative - this is why the proposal should be shelved."

E tū team leader Cathie Powell said security guards were keeping people safe.

"It doesn't make sense to us why you would reduce security - at a time when there are more and more people feeling the stress of unemployment, the rising cost of living.

"It doesn't seem like this is the right time to making cuts in these core service places."

Staff in hundreds of lockdowns, face thousands of security incidents each year

Ministry of Social Development data, released to RNZ under the Official Information Act, shows Work and Income staff faced 14,420 security incidents over the past five years.

Moderate security incidents at offices, without injury, ranged from 708 in 2021 to 1373 in 2025 - spiking in 2024 at 1387 incidents.

But the numbers of security incidents involving a weapon at offices increased - growing from 30 in 2021 to 47 in 2025.

Severe security incidents peaked in 2022 at 12, dropping to four in 2025.

Overall, staff went into lockdown in offices 1736 times over the past five years - reaching 544 lockdowns in 2024, and 441 in 2025.

PSA national secretary Fleur Fitzsimons. Supplied

Our offices are safer than they were - MSD

Ministry of Social Development's deputy chief executive, Melissa Gill, said the agency had invested $80m to make sites safer, including in the layout of offices, and through boosting training.

The programme of work was a direct response to the WorkSafe court judgment - and now was the right time to make changes.

She said the vast majority of interactions with Work and Income clients were positive.

Gill said it wasn't true that staff were under-reporting incidents - and they were encouraged to report all, no matter how serious.

But she said there were fewer incidents involving damage, physical injuries or lockdowns.

"Between 2023 and 2025 our staff reported 11.6 percent more security events. Over the same period, the number of severe security events reduced by more than half."

Gill said reducing the number of guards in March had "gone smoothly", and hadn't affected the way security incidents were handled.

She said no decisions had been made over this proposal, and staff could provide feedback. Consultation was due to end on 12 August.

"The safety and security of the public and staff at our sites remains incredibly important to us. We're making changes because it is safe to do so. This is based on site-by-site risk assessments."

The Minister for Social Development, Louise Upston, said the security guard proposal was an operational matter, and she was confident officials prioritised safety.

World.title: Transpower expecting record electricity demand in cold snap
World.content:
Transpower is expecting record demand for electricity this week as cold weather grips the country.

It told power generators on Monday there could be potential shortfalls on Wednesday morning and evening and again on Thursday morning.

Transpower executive general manager operations Chantelle Bramley told RNZ the industry responded to that notice.

"We're monitoring the situation closely and the industry has responded as anticipated to resolve potential low residuals across the peak morning and evening periods on Wednesday," she said.

"We are continuing to liaise with the industry to ensure there is enough generation being offered to meet what is forecast to be record electricity demand through the rest of the week."

Bramley said Monday's notice was made "to ensure the electricity industry was aware of the potential for a tight balance between supply and demand during this cold snap. These notices are part of our standard operating process."

She said Transpower was not expecting any impact on electricity supply for consumers.

"If the situation tightens further across the coming days we will issue additional notices as per established procedures with industry," she said.

World.title: ACT's 'visually misleading' post: Is it a graphic or a graph?
World.content:
An ACT Party post about the gap between new medicines funded in Australia and New Zealand is "visually misleading," according to a statistics professor.

The post on the ACT party's Facebook page shows two stacks of pills and says Australia has funded 215 medicines between 2011 and 2025, while New Zealand has funded 86. Australia is represented with a stack of 10 pills and New Zealand has just two pills.

Professor Thomas Lumley, a biostatistician at the University of Auckland, says the difference between the pill stacks depicted is 5 times, when it should be 2.5 times.

The ACT party's press secretary for Todd Stephenson denied the post was misleading saying it was a "graphic and not a graph". It aimed to show the gap between Australia and New Zealand's funding of new medicines.

But most people would interpret the graphic as a graph, according to Lumley, who said it was "clearly giving bar charts".

"People do graphs like that, it's a decorative way of doing a bar graph."

People viewing it this way would have an incorrect reading of the actual difference, he said.

"I would say this ad is visually misleading."

He couldn't say if it was poor design, or deliberate.

"It may even be deliberate in taking advantage of the fact it can be passed off as bad design."

Presenting numerical data inaccurately detracted from meaningful political discussion, Lumley said.

RNZ could not independently verify the medicine figures in the post, and ACT did not cite a source.

X (formerly Twitter)

Dylan Reeve takes an interest in disinformation and is the author of Fake Believe: Conspiracy Theories in Aotearoa.

In 2019 he complained to the Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) about a National party  relating to fuel prices.

The ad also included a bar chart which was incorrectly scaled and visually exaggerated the price under Labour. The  was eventually ruled as acceptable, although the ASA labelled it "mischievous" and said it had the potential to cause confusion.

The ASA assesses advocacy advertising, which includes political advertising, differently to other types of advertising. It says this is because the ads promote the view of the advertiser, rather than a product or service.

It makes an allowance for opinion, as long as opinion is clearly separated from fact.

At the time, its chief executive Hilary Souter told RNZ she agreed the graph bars didn't match the numbers but that this was National's interpretation of information: "The majority of the board felt the numbers in this ad were very clear, it's impossible to miss them even if you choose to also at look the representation of these bars."

Policing our politicians for porkies The Detail Download MP3 24m

Reeve, however, said political parties should hold their advertising to a high standard.

"It's being carried out by people who are asking us to trust them with the operation of the country. I think we should demand of them accuracy, honesty and forthrightness in how they make that pitch to us."

Reeve agreed most people would interpret ACT's post as a chart because it used the "language of data".

"You've got one big stack, and one small stack. You look at that and go, those are comparable."

With two pills representing 86 medicines for New Zealand, the ten pills representing Australia would equate to 430 medicines, far greater than the 215 the sign on the pile of pills states.

ACT's post was not a paid . At present, social media posts don't fall under the remit of the ASA, but Reeve felt other advertising circulating at present, such as National's s stating "Triple your taxes" could mislead people.

The ASA has received 72 complaints about National's tax tripling ads, but has not upheld them saying the ad is a statement of political opinion. All of its five decisions this year related to political ads have involved National. One complaint was settled and the remaining four weren't upheld. Souter said the ASA has not received any complaints about ACT's post.

ACT also hasn't received direct complaints about the depiction of pills in its post.

World.title: Our Changing World: High powered magnets, and making steel with hydrogen
World.content:
High powered magnets, and making steel with hydrogen Our Changing World Download MP3 25m

Follow Our Changing World on Apple, Spotify, iHeartRadio or wherever you listen to your podcasts

New Zealand researchers are developing a new way to make steel that could dramatically reduce carbon emissions while making use of the country's distinctive black ironsands.

At the Paihau Robinson Research Institute at Victoria University of Wellington, Professor Chris Bumby and his team have spent close to a decade investigating how hydrogen could replace coal in one of the most carbon-intensive industrial processes in the world.

"Steel is also responsible for about seven and a half percent of the total world's CO2 emissions," says Chris. "And in New Zealand it's a very significant amount of our total industrial emissions is coming from the Glenbrook steel plant."

Traditionally, steel production relies on the carbon in coal to remove oxygen from iron ore.

Coked coal, iron oxide and some limestone is heated in a blast furnace, the oxygen gets stripped from the ore, and the iron melts, separating out into pig-iron and slag (leftover material). The process has been used for centuries, but it produces large quantities of carbon dioxide as a by-product.

In New Zealand, the process is more challenging.

New Zealand's black sands

"We have a somewhat unusual iron ore. We use iron sand," says Chris.

The iron-rich black sands found along parts of the North Island's West Coast provide one of the raw ingredients for New Zealand steelmaking.

RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

However, they also contain titanium dioxide (TiO2), which prevents them from being processed in conventional blast furnaces, Chris explains "What happens is that if you try and just melt that in a blast furnace that TiO2 has a very high melting point well above two thousand degrees C, and that doesn't flow through your blast furnace. So it just solidifies your entire blast furnace as one big ceramic terracotta ornament."

Instead, New Zealand steelmaking relies on a bespoke method developed in the 1960s, which involves a two-step process to make iron.

In the first stage the iron oxide in the black sands is 'reduced' by using heat and coal to strip oxygen away, producing what's called direct reduced iron.

The Robinson Research Institute team have targeted this step, using hydrogen rather than carbon (the coal) to do this chemical stripping of oxygen. Instead of producing a carbon dioxide byproduct, this reaction makes water. If a source of 'green' hydrogen could be used, this would dramatically reduce the emissions footprint of the process.

To test the concept, the researchers have built a series of increasingly larger reactors. What began as gram-scale experiments has grown to laboratory pilot reactors capable of producing around 10 kilograms of direct reduced iron per hour.

The before and after looks very similar to the naked eye.

The team have been working through the steps to figure out how to make steel using New Zealand iron sand without burning coal. Claire Concannon

"It's a little bit disappointing in that we're putting black sand in and we're getting black sand out," senior research engineer Ben Rumsey says. "But I can tell you a lot has changed."

Scaling up the reactors has allowed the team to produce more direct reduced iron, which they can then melt and test the chemistry of. Because they are using hydrogen instead of carbon, their resulting iron product will be different to traditional pig iron, and will need to be treated differently in the subsequent steps of steel-making.

Not just reducing carbon emissions

As they worked through this process a key discovery has been that the hydrogen reaction is dramatically faster than the traditional coal-based process.

In the Glenbrook steel mill it can take about 10 hours to convert the iron sand to direct reduced iron.

"We can achieve that same reaction in about two and a half minutes using hydrogen", says Professor Chris Bumby.

That increase in speed could offer significant commercial advantages, allowing more material to be processed in a much smaller footprint.

As a result, the research has begun the move beyond the laboratory.

CullBeck staff at Glenbrook Steel Mill: Chris Bumby, Chris Jansen, Martin Hacon, Bavinesh Maisuria Supplied by CullBeck

A new company, CullBeck Limited, has been established to commercialise the technology and is working towards building a larger demonstration facility next to the Glenbrook Steel Mill.

While New Zealand's ironsands prompted the research, the technology could have applications elsewhere. Similar titanomagnetite sand deposits occur in other parts of the world, particularly around the 'Pacific Ring of Fire'.

World.title: NRLW great Ali Brigginshaw gets three-match ban
World.content:
Brisbane Broncos skipper Ali Brigginshaw has been handed a three-week ban for a dangerous tackle and will miss a major chunk of the rest of the NRLW home-and-away season.

Brigginshaw was sent straight to the judiciary for her tackle on Canterbury's Tayla Preston during Magic Round at Wagga Wagga.

The Broncos lead the competition with a 5-0 record, but Brigginshaw will now be unavailable until round 9, three games before the finals series.

As Preston ran the ball away from her goal line, Brigginshaw advanced and grabbed the Bulldogs player, then spun her around before lifting her up and bringing her down on her head.

Preston avoided serious injury and Brigginshaw was charged with a grade 3 dangerous throw.

Brigginshaw thanked the judiciary panel for considering her case and reiterated her remorse for the incident.

"I meant absolutely no malice in making the tackle, I apologised to Tayla post-match and have been in contact with her again since, she was accepting of my apology on both occasions," she said.

"I'm looking forward to getting back on the field in a few weeks and finishing my playing career on a positive note."

The 36-year-old, who is playing her final season of NRLW before retirement, has not missed a Broncos game since the competition's inception in 2018.

Sydney Roosters forward Aliyah Nasio was the last NRLW player to be referred directly to the judiciary following a brawl at the conclusion of last year's grand final, when she struck Brisbane's Julia Robinson.

Nasio was banned for four matches after being hit with a grade 3 striking charge.

In 2023, Parramatta's Kennedy Cherrington was also banned for four weeks after being charged with a grade 3 dangerous throw.

World.title: Clarkson happy with handshake to extend contract as North set to miss finals
World.content:
North Melbourne coach Alastair Clarkson is unfazed going into the final year of his contract, saying he just needs a "handshake".

As Clarkson comes towards the end of his fourth season in charge, North will spend a 10th-straight year without experiencing finals action.

Speculation has started to mount that Kangaroos hierarchy might consider letting Clarkson go at the end of his current five-year deal, signed in late 2022 in what was a massive coup for the club.

Although North have improved this year, they are yet to beat a team above them on the ladder and will fall short of a wildcard berth.

AFL round 21 Saturday live updates Josh Fraser's bid to become Carlton's next full-time coach receives a massive boost as the Blues record a thumping win over the Brisbane Lions.

"Old school" Clarkson will not be pushing for a contract extension beyond 2027 this off-season and is happy to wait it out.

"All I require is a handshake and a wink and a nod, and that'll do me," the four-time Hawthorn premiership coach said on Tuesday.

"We'll work our way through whatever we need to do.

"I'm really here to serve the footy club … it's not just me, but those that are in leadership positions at the club have done a really good job stabilising the footy club.

"We're really keen to progress and get ourselves up the ladder, but all we do know is that that's done best when you've got stability."

Clarkson drew on examples of Brisbane Lions, Fremantle and Adelaide of clubs who were patient with their coaches and find themselves in powerful positions on the field.

"I've been in the caper for a long time, so that's a bit of water off the duck's (back)," he said of speculation about his future.

"The best examples are the reigning premiers (Brisbane) who took a while to get going and then Adelaide with 'Nicksy' (Matthew Nicks) and Fremantle with Justin Longmuir.

"The governance and administration of the club just sticking to the path and sticking to the course, and we're going to be no different."

Clarkson's record at North is 19-1-59, a far cry from his glory years with the Hawks.

The Kangaroos face a challenging run home, starting with the Western Bulldogs at Docklands on Thursday night.

They have long losing streaks against the Bulldogs, and their final two opponents, Geelong and Sydney.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Clarkson bristled when asked how important it would be to beat one of those teams to finish off this season.

"You're just searching, searching for a headline," he said.

"Teams that have been in the bottom four or five on the ladder haven't beaten the top teams very often in the last five or six years.

"That's the reason why they've been in that position on the ladder."

AAP

World.title: Clubs stand firm after AFL's controversial finals memo
World.content:
The AFL's warning to clubs about resting players before the newly introduced wildcard round has not gone down well with coaches.

Clubs have been threatened with sanctions if they decide to make mass changes for their games in round 24.

"While legitimate player management of player fatigue or injuries is permitted, the AFL will scrutinise club team selection decisions in the lead-up to AFL finals," AFL football boss Greg Swann wrote in a memo to clubs on Monday.

The AFL has had a pre-finals bye since 2016, allowing the top-eight teams a week off before the last month of the season.

But with the finals system effectively becoming a top-10 due to the wildcard weekend, not every club will be afforded that luxury should they qualify.

Teams ranked seventh to 10th at the end of the home-and-away season will have to back up and play the following week.

The top-six will all rest before preparing for respective qualifying and elimination finals, starting on September 3.

The Western Bulldogs are almost certain to finish in the wildcard bracket, creating a dilemma for coach Luke Beveridge.

"The main consideration for the teams who might be certainties to play a wildcard game going into that round is the fact that the six teams above the seventh have all got a week off," Beveridge told Fox Footy.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"I'm sure within the ranks of the teams that are certainties, you're processing who needs a week off.

"I'd question how the AFL could question a club, because you're questioning the medical department from a club as well, if that happens."

Steven King, in his rookie season as Melbourne coach, was also left perplexed by the AFL's directive.

"I'm the coach of the Melbourne footy club," he told Fox Footy.

"I'll make any decision that's best for our football club and best for the management of our players."

The Dockers made a string of changes for the last home-and-away round in 2013, then travelled to Geelong and beat the Cats in finals. (Getty Images: Michael Dodge)

Fremantle famously made 10 changes for their final home-and-away game in 2013, leading to them being thrashed by struggling St Kilda.

The following week, the Dockers pulled off a historic qualifying-final win in Geelong over the highly fancied Cats.

In 2015, North Melbourne rested nine players ahead of a finals campaign when they lost against Richmond.

The move paid off for the Kangaroos, who turned the tables on the Tigers in an elimination final and also won a semi-final in Sydney.

Former North Melbourne coach Brad Scott rested nine players in the final round of the 2015 season, while Ross Lyon made 10 changes in the final round of the 2013 season when he was in charge of Fremantle.

AAP

World.title: Aussie swimmer out of leadership group after reported drinking session
World.content:
Australian swimmer Isaac Cooper has stepped down from the Dolphins's leadership group after a drinking session at the Commonwealth Games.

Cooper was reported to be out drinking when he was expected to be supporting teammates at Glasgow's Tollcross International Swimming Centre last Wednesday night.

Cooper was also seen drinking at the Australian team hotel during that day, the report said.

"Isaac did not attend the final night of the swimming competition or final team meeting in Glasgow, which is in conflict with team expectations," a Swimming Australia statement said.

What the Commonwealth Games mean is up to you Australian chef de mission and eight-time Olympic medallist Petria Thomas cried as she spoke about the importance of the Commonwealth Games to her, so it doesn't really matter if it felt too easy for Australia at times.

"Isaac has since voluntarily stood down from the team's athlete leadership group."

Cooper was scheduled to race the 100m backstroke final that night but withdrew from the event after qualifying eighth-fastest.

Swimmers were expected to support teammates at the Glasgow Games when not racing, while Cooper also missed the team meeting that night.

The 22-year-old won gold at the Glasgow Games as a member of the 4x100m medley team after swimming in the heats.

He also finished sixth in the 50m backstroke final, an event he won a silver medal at the 2024 world championships.

Cooper will next compete at the Pan Pacific championships in the United States starting August 12.

AAP

World.title: Blues announce King as new Origin coach after Daley steps down
World.content:
Former NSW State of Origin player Matt King has been named the new head coach of the Blues.

King was announced as the new coach on Tuesday after predecessor Laurie Daley stepped down from the role on Monday.

Blues pay tribute to 'hero' Daley as he stands down as coach The NSWRL pays tribute to Blues "hero" Laurie Daley as the coach stands down from his role after this year's series win over Queensland.

King played nine times for the Blues from 2005-2007, and over 200 first grade matches for Melbourne, South Sydney and Warrington across the NRL and Super League in England.

"I'm very clear on what it looks like to be the head coach of NSW," King said.

"I have a true understanding of what it means to lead this great state of ours and I can't wait for that opportunity.

"The one true rugby league love of my life has been the NSW Blues. To know now that I have the opportunity to guide the team moving forward, to lead the program over the next little period, means the absolute world to me."

The 45-year-old has been a long-time assistant coach under Trent Robinson at the Sydney Roosters, and has been part of the Blues' coaching staff since 2024.

Daley stepped down as Blues coach on Monday after guiding NSW to a series win this year.

The Blues sealed the series with a 30-12 triumph in the decider at Lang Park, just the fourth time NSW has won a deciding Game III in Brisbane.

Daley slams 'hidden agendas' after NSW Origin win Laurie Daley has the last laugh over critics who hounded him ahead of the State of Origin decider at Lang Park.

"I've always considered it an absolute honour and privilege to be involved with the NSW Blues State of Origin team, whether that was as a player or a coach, and I've always been ready to answer the call for my state whenever they needed me," Daley said in a statement on Monday.

"We faced plenty of challenges in the 2026 series and I'm proud of the way the players banded together to overcome them and save their best performance for Game Three in Brisbane to secure a memorable series win.

"I thank the fans for their passion and their support, and I can't think of a better way to move on with the Shield back where it belongs in NSW."

World.title: Haugset goes it alone to claim Tour de France Femmes third stage
World.content:
Sigrid Haugset has set off on a long solo run and kept going to the finish to win the third stage of the Women's Tour de France and claim the yellow jersey.

The Norwegian rider made her break with more than half of the tough 156.5-kilometre route between Geneva and Poligny to go.

The stage featured four categorised climbs and Haugset made her move with 85 kilometres left, at the foot of the category two Col de la Savine.

Haugset was also first across the last listed climb of the day, the category four Côte de Chaux-Champagny, followed by Lotte Kopecky about 30 seconds behind, and a nine-rider group more than two minutes adrift.

Previous yellow jersey holder Lorena Wiebes, who won the first two stages, was 13 minutes behind with the main bunch at the time. She ultimately finished more than 20 minutes adrift of Haugset and dropped to 67th in the general classification.

It was a battle between two riders going into the last 10 kilometres. Kopecky had cut Haugset's lead to 15 seconds and the Belgian rider could just about see her rival ahead.

But Haugset, sensing the danger, stood on her pedals to stay ahead and managed to increase her lead again, finishing 1:24 ahead of Kopecky.

Haugset leads the general classification by 2:02 from Kimberley Le Court of Mauritius, with 2023 Tour champion Demi Vollering third, a further four seconds behind.

This edition of the race, the fifth of the Women's Tour, covers 1,175 kilometres over nine days.

World.title: Infantino could face UEFA lawsuit as he scrambles for FIFA presidency support
World.content:
European football body UEFA has threatened FIFA with legal action over Gianni Infantino's failed plan to sell a stake in future World Cup profits to private investors, and says potential evidence should not be destroyed.

Mr Infantino on Saturday dropped a secretive proposal to raise $US4.2 billion ($6 billion) from investors, including the New York investment firm of Joshua Kushner, days after media reports revealed it, provoking a global furore.

UEFA led the backlash and its 55 member federations met to agree to boycott all FIFA events and competitions while the proposal was active.

Now UEFA's lawyers have informed FIFA that the European body is "actively considering legal action, arbitration, and/or regulatory complaints … arising out of and in connection with the FFE (FIFA Forward Enterprise) plan proposed by FIFA and all related matters".

The letter named 18 FIFA executives who it said should retain data, documents and electronic messages as potential evidence. They include Mr Infantino, Zurich-based chief finance officer Thomas Peyer and Arsène Wenger, the coaching great who is FIFA's head of global football development.

Football bodies launch stunning Infantino rebuke Two of football's major bodies launch stinging rebukes of FIFA boss Gianni Infantino after his failed privatisation ploy.

"UEFA puts you on formal notice that any destruction, deletion, alteration, concealment, or loss of relevant materials following receipt of this notice — or following any earlier date on which you were, or reasonably should have been, aware that proceedings were anticipated — may constitute spoliation of evidence," the letter said.

Meanwhile, the Swedish football federation confirmed that UEFA is actively looking "to come up with an alternative candidate" as FIFA president. The next election is scheduled in March.

On Saturday, UEFA signalled it wants to end Mr Infantino's decade-long presidency, saying he had lost the confidence of world football and that "no option should be off the table".

Hours earlier, Mr Infantino had withdrawn the divisive proposal that offered FIFA's 211 member federations one-off payments of $20 million each with a mid-September deadline to accept.

The FFE spin-off valued by FIFA at $20 billion would have taken control of the football body's money-making commercial and tournament operations through at least 2038. It promised to more than double development money over that time for the 211 members who already effectively own the Zurich-based not-for-profit governing body.

It was the project of just one man, FIFA's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said in a stinging statement that said staff felt deceived by their boss Mr Infantino.

FIFA COO Kevin Lamour has made clear his opposition to Gianni Infantino's plan. (Getty Images: Joosep Martinson)

Legal proceedings are "reasonably anticipated," UEFA's lawyer Andrew J Levander wrote, citing the belief of football stakeholders that the plan was "fundamentally incompatible with the proper governance of football".

UEFA has been outspoken against its former employee Mr Infantino, while the Asian Football Confederation and CONCACAF also made strong statements opposing Mr Infantino's plan.

Mr Infantino has most support from his traditional base in Africa, while South America's CONMEBOL is relying on him to expand the 2030 World Cup to 64 teams from 48. That would give more hosting games to Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay, the home country of CONMEBOL president Alejandro Dominguez.

Gianni Infantino is reportedly seeking support from Donald Trump in his FIFA presidency battle. (Reuters: Dylan Martinez)

Mr Infantino's path to stabilising the presidency he has held for more than 10 years was unclear. A report yesterday claimed he was seeking support from the administration of his close ally US President Donald Trump, possibly in a call with Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

"There are no plans for @SecRubio to speak with Mr Infantino and there is no call this morning," Dylan Johnson, assistant secretary of state for global public affairs, posted on social media.

The 56-year-old FIFA leader left New York after the World Cup final two weeks ago seemingly a lock to be re-elected unopposed next March for a fourth and final term in office through 2031.

FIFA briefed at the World Cup that Mr Infantino had pledged letters of support from about 200 of the 211 member federations.

Those letters are now likely being withdrawn across Europe, with the Wales federation the first to announce its reversal.

The candidate deadline is November 18 for an election four months later in Morocco.
